I'm still concerned about this. And Elar you have other things to do and I am ok if you ignore this. But here is one last attempt at an argument here.

There are several other scenarios where an uploaded file can be unexpectedly executed, depending on the environment, platform, and misconfigurations. Modern platforms can execute files more dynamically.

A. Files Executed via Web Server Behavior
	•	Misconfigured servers (Apache, Nginx, IIS) might treat uploaded files as scripts based on:
	•	File extension (e.g., .php, .jsp, .aspx)
	•	MIME type sniffing
	•	Script handler mappings (e.g., Apache’s AddHandler)
	•	Path traversal bugs can allow attackers to upload to locations outside of intended directories (e.g., /var/www/html/admin/)

B. Files Placed in Executable Paths
	•	If uploaded files end up in a path that is:
	•	Scanned by the runtime or container, such as:
	•	Python’s PYTHONPATH
	•	Java’s classpath
	•	Node’s require() resolution directories
	•	Served from a script-enabled directory, such as a .php file in /uploads with AllowOverride All

C. Files Triggered by Extensions or Applications
	•	Image upload with embedded script (e.g., polyglot file: valid image + PHP code)
	•	Office documents with macros (e.g., .docm, .xlsm)
	•	Executable installers, .exe, .msi, .app, when opened on user systems
	•	Shell scripts that get run by automation systems (e.g., uploaded .sh picked up by CI/CD)

D. Archive Uploads That Get Extracted
	•	ZIP or TAR files uploaded, then extracted server-side without sanitization, can:
	•	Place files in sensitive locations (../ traversal in zip)
	•	Inject executable code into other files (e.g., override .bashrc)
	•	Exploit symlinks in the archive

E. File Parsing Libraries with RCE or DoS Vulnerabilities
	•	ImageMagick (“ImageTragick”), ExifTool, FFmpeg, etc., have had critical RCE bugs triggered during parsing of malicious files.

F. Uploaded Files Interpreted by External Services
	•	PDFs or images uploaded to a server might be sent to third-party OCR/analysis APIs, where parsing could be exploited
	•	Serverless functions that process uploaded files may have poor sandboxing

G. Content Embedding in Trusted Contexts
	•	Uploaded SVG files embedded inline in HTML can run inline JavaScript
	•	Uploaded files reused in email templates, user profile pages, etc., may enable stored XSS or template injection

So I'd suggest:

_Verify that uploaded files are not executed, interpreted, or otherwise processed as code by the application, server, or any downstream system, regardless of upload location. This includes scenarios involving direct URL access, inclusion in server-side processing pipelines, or automatic extraction and handling._

⸻

Best Practices for Uploads (Defense-in-Depth)
	1.	Store uploads outside the web root or with execution disabled (noexec mount, restrictive server configs)
	2.	Rename files and drop extensions (uuid.data instead of backdoor.php)
	3.	Enforce strong file type validation (based on magic bytes, not just MIME or extension)
	4.	Avoid server-side processing of files unless absolutely necessary
	5.	Use CSP + sandboxing when embedding uploaded content in a browser context
	6.	Log and monitor file uploads and access patterns

I get the point of "RCE is an impact, not the cause". I see where you are coming from. It's a fair point.

But let me try again from a different perspective.

In traditional web hosting (Apache, Nginx static file serving, PHP apps, etc.), the "public folder" was the root directory exposed directly to the browser, everything in it was world-readable, and anything outside of it was considered application or server logic and protected by the web server.

Modern frameworks like Next.js, Spring, Laravel, Django, Ruby on Rails and others still often include a public or static directory, **_but the usage has changed:_**

**1. Static assets are explicitly handled**
- Frameworks bundle and compile assets during build time.
- Static files go to a public/ or static/ folder (e.g. images, CSS, JS).
- These files are served via CDN or web server as raw files.

**2. App logic is not exposed publicly**

- App routes are compiled into server-side code or API routes.
- Files and routes are protected by the runtime (e.g., Node.js server, serverless function handlers).
- Files are often inside a /pages, /routes, or /src folder—not directly exposed to the public.

**3. Deployment platforms further abstract "public"**
Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda, and others:
- Build the app and deploy only needed static files to an edge/CDN.
- Dynamically generate server-side content from handlers.
- Make "public" a conceptual boundary, not necessarily a filesystem one.

This is why I don't like the term "public folder" - modern frameworks and deployment pipelines use this idea more logically than literally now, with dynamic content rendered securely and separated from public exposure. And that makes file upload dangers a lot different than the PHP days of public folder.
